### page_1
PALEOMAGNETISM IN ABITIBI GREENSTONE BELT, AND 
ABITIBI AND MATACHEWAN DIABASE DIKES: 
EVIDENCE OF THE ARCHEAN GEOMAGNETIC FIELD1,2 
E. IRVING AND A. J. NALDRETT 
Earth Physics Branch, Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, Ottawa and 
Department of Geology, University of Toronto, Toronto 
ABSTRACT 
Paleomagnetic results are described from three Archean rock units, and two sets of diabase dikes 
that intrude them. The magnetization of the country rocks is reset by intrusion of the diabase up to 
distances of about 80 m from contacts. The temperature reached during intrusion at this distance 
determined from thermal demagnetization is about 400°C, which is also the approximate temperature 
predicted from Jaeger's cooling curves assuming intrusion into cool rock. At greater distances other 
and presumably older magnetizations are found with a westerly direction. The oldest dykes (the 
Matachewan) have an age of - 2.6 Ga so that this westerly directed magnetization was acquired 
during the Archean. Its age, other than the fact that it is Archean, is not known, but by comparison 
with results from the Stillwater Complex it is estimated to be about - 2.8 Ga. The results are used 
along with previously published data to define in tentative fashion an apparent polar wandering 
curve for the late Archean and early Aphebian which is referred to as Track 6. Track 6 has a simple 
form, and there is no indication that the horizontal mobility of the crust in the late Archean was 
any greater than during the Proterozoic. 
INTRODUCTION 
The purpose of this paper is to describe 
new paleomagnetic results from the Abitibi 
Greenstone Belt, and then to use them to 
construct a path of apparent polar wander 
(APW) for late Archean and early Aphe- 
bian time (approximately -2.3 to -2.8 
Ga, Ga = 109y). This polar path is of 
potential importance for stratigraphic 
correlations and for the tectonic history of 
late Archean time. For instance, it would 
provide information relating to the nature 
of the Kenoran Orogeny. Sampling was 
carried out during the summers of 1970, 
1971, and 1973. 
The Abitibi greenstone belt is relatively 
weakly metamorphosed, the grade of 
metamorphism varying from lower green- 
schist to prehnite-pumpellyite facies (Jolly 
1974). In Munro township, where much of 
our work has been done, it is prehnite- 
pumpellyite (Arndt et al. 1977). Because 
the rocks have undergone only low-grade 
metamorphism it does not necessarily 
1 Manuscript received July 12, 1976; revised 
October 5, 1976. 
2 Earth Physics Branch Contribution No. 639. 
[JOURNAL OF GEOLOGY, 1977, Vol. 85, p. 157-176] 
© 1977 by the University of Chicago. All rights reserved. 
follow that their original magnetizations 
have been retained. Rocks that are 
essentially unaltered geologically, can have 
had their original magnetization replaced 
partly or entirely by secondary magnetiza- 
tion. This phenomenon of partial or 
complete resetting of magnetizations is 
widespread in Precambrian terrains. (See 
documentation of magnetic overprints, 
figs. 9, 10, and 11, Irving and McGlynn 
1976.) The temperatures achieved during 
low-grade metamorphism (say 300°C) are 
lower than the blocking temperature of 
rocks commonly observed on laboratory 
time scales (typically 500 to 600°C), but 
magnetization can be destroyed if these 
temperatures are applied for long intervals 
of time. Time itself becomes an effective 
agent of demagnetization. Such secondary 
magnetization has been shown by blocking 
temperatures, ranging from the Curie 
temperature of the constituent minerals 
down to room temperatures, whereas the 
magnetization that has survived is 
characterized by a small discrete range of 
blocking temperatures withih 50° or so of 
the Curie temperature. The theoretical 
explanation of this phenomenon has 
recently been given by Buchan and 
157

### page_2
E. IRVING AND A. J. NALDRETT 
Dunlop (in Pullaiah et al. 1975). The 
magnetization of single-domain pure mag- 
netite and hematite should survive the 
prehnite-pumpellyite and low greenschist 
facies metamorphism provided there has 
been no chemical change of the iron 
minerals. It ought to be possible to 
retrieve original magnetizations in the 
Abitibi Greenstone Belt provided that 
magnetizations with high discrete blocking 
temperatures (that is square-shouldered 
thermal decay curves) can be located. The 
key observations required are the thermal 
decay characteristics. 
The metamorphism associated with the 
Kenoran Orogeny, is however not the only 
possible cause of remagnetization. Long- 
term mild reheating may have accom- 
panied either the intrusion of Proterozoic 
dikes, or burial beneath Huronian sedi- 
ments which may once have blanketed 
this area. Thus studies of dike contacts 
have been made, and one of the by- 
products of this work has been that we 
have been able to show, for the first time, 
that the characteristic magnetization di- 
rections of the Abitibi and Matachewan 
dike swarms were acquired at the time 
they were intruded. 
The first important study of palaeo- 
magnetism of Archean rocks of Laurentia 
was made by Berg (1970) on the Stillwater 
Igneous Complex. Estimates of the age of 
emplacement of the complex have been 
obtained by Nunes and Tilton (1971) who 
obtained -2.75 Ga by the U-Pb method 
from zircons in the basal zone, and by 
Mueller and Wooden (1976) who obtained 
-2.75 + 0.05 Ga for an Rb-Sr isochron 
from the contact aureole. (Rb-Sr ages in 
this paper are quoted for SRb decay 
constant of 1.39 x 10-11y-1.) Berg ob- 
tained some consistent magnetization 
directions, but the layering at his sites is 
approximately uniform so that it is not 
possible to use Graham's fold test (Graham 
1949) to determine whether the magnetiza- 
tion was acquired before or after deforma- 
tion. Berg believed that the magnetization 
was acquired before deformation. It is 
equally possible that the magnetization 
was acquired after deformation. For 
example the thick Archean sills of the 
Chibougamau Greenstone Belt have mag- 
netizations which structural evidence 
shows were acquired after deformation 
(Ueno and Irving 1976). Ueno and Irving 
therefore considered these magnetizations 
to be somewhat younger than the Kenoran 
Orogeny, which in this area is determined 
by Rb-Sr isochrons to be about -2.6 Ga 
(Jones et al. 1974). Ridler and Foster 
(1975) have given results in abstract from 
the Skead Group. Although they do not 
report any thermal studies, they do report 
that they have carried out a fold test 
indicating that the magnetization is 
Archean in age. Symons (1967) has 
reported work on the Ely greenstones of 
Minnesota but no thermal studies were 
made and only nine samples studied; the 
data do not fulfil the minimum reliability 
criteria of Hicken et al. (1972) and are 
therefore not considered further in this 
paper. Preliminary results have been 
reported from the Shebandowan volcanic- 
plutonic belt at the Superior Geotraverse 
Conferences by Dunlop and Buchan (1975, 
1976) and by Halls (1975), and abstracts 
of work by Londry and Symons (1976) and 
Dunlop and Buchan (1976) have appeared 
but no thermal studies have been reported, 
and the results are not therefore con- 
sidered further in this paper. 
REGIONAL GEOLOGY 
Goodwin and Ridler (1970) have defined 
the Abitibi Greenstone Belt as a crudely 
parallelogram-shaped structure extending 
from the Grenville Front in the east 
through Noranda and Timmins to the 
belt of gneisses associated with the 
Kapuskasing gravity high in the west. It 
is bounded to north and south by areas of 
metasedimentary and gneissic rocks, which 
are intruded by a variety of felsic plutons, 
one of which was dated by Krogh and 
Davis (1971) at -2.7 Ga using the U-Pb 
method on zircons. Much of our work has 
been in Munro and Dundonald townships

FIG. 1.-Sketch-match of sampling region taken from Ontario Geological Map No. 2198. A = Mafic 
and ultramafic intrusives, metavolcanics and metasediments; B = granitic rocks; 0 = Huronian sed- 
iments; D = diabase dikes; KGB =- Kapuskasing gneiss belt. The northeast trending dikes are of 
the Abitibi swarm. The north-south dikes belong to the Matachewan swarm. The sampling sites are 
numbered. 
in the western part of the belt (fig. 1). In 
the vicinity of Munro, the oldest rocks 
constitute a dominantly south-facing suc- 
cession and occur within and to the north 
of the township. They belong to the 
Kinojevis Group (Dimroth et al. 1973; 
Jensen, in prep.) and consist largely of 
Fe-rich tholeiitic basalts with a small 
proportion of intermediate to felsic vol- 
canic rock, and a succession of ultramafic 
lavas and mafic-ultramafic intrusions 
which are referred to by Arndt et al. 
(1977) as the Munro Formation. The 
Kinojevis Group is overlain by the Blake 
River Group, a thick succession of 
dominantly calc-alkaline volcanic rocks 
that outcrop over a large, crudely elliptical 
area extending from Nighthawk Lake in 
the west to east of Noranda. The Blake 
River Group is overlain by the Skead 
Group. 
In Munro and adjacent townships the 
Munro Formation has been folded about 
east-southeast trending axes and disrupted 
by a series of early faults with similar 
strike. Gabbros have been injected along 
these faults and, at first sight, appear to be 
concordant, although Arndt (1976) has 
demonstrated that they cut across con- 
cordant strata of the Munro Formation at 
the noses of folds. These fault-controlled 
gabbros are cut by north-south dikes of 
Matachewan age (-2.69 ± 0.93 Ga, Gates 
and Hurley 1973) which, in turn, are cut 
by east-northeast trending Abitibi dikes. 
The latter have yielded an Rb-Sr isochron 
of -2.15 ± 0.68 Ga (Gates and Hurley 
1973). 
159

### page_4
E. IRVING AND A. J. NALDRETT 
The Dundonald sill (Naldrett and 
Mason 1968), sampled by us in Dundonald 
township 50 km west of Munro, is identical 
to the sills in Munro township (MacRae 
1969), and probably lies within the Munro 
Formation, although poor outcrop and 
complex structure in the intervening area 
leave this an open question. The Kamis- 
kotia complex sampled in Robb township 
15 km northwest of Timmins, differs from 
the sills of Munro and Dundonald town- 
ships in that it contains less peridotite and 
pyroxenite and more anorthositic gabbro. 
It is intrusive into a volcanic succession 
that is capped by felsic rocks. Poor 
outcrop has prevented correlation of this 
succession with rocks east of Timmins. 
The Kamiskotia complex belongs petro- 
logically to a group of anorthositic 
magnetite rich intrusions including the 
Dord Lake and Bell River complexes 
(Class I subclass ii(b) of Naldrett and 
Cabri 1976), which are probably com- 
parable in age to the basement. 
METHODS 
Samples were cored by gasoline drill and 
oriented by magnetic and solar compass. 
About five cores were drilled at each 
collecting site, and two cylindrical speci- 
mens were cut from each core. The 
remanent magnetization of the specimens 
was measured by spinner magnetometers. 
All specimens were demagnetized by 
step-wise heating, or by alternating fields 
(a.f. peak field strength are quoted) using 
the apparatus described by Roy et al. 
(1969, 1971, 1973). Demagnetization was 
carried in fields of less than two gammas. 
In some samples, particularly from the 
Dundonald sill, no coherent magnetization 
could be found; if the directions in 
specimens from the same sample disagreed 
by more than 40°, the results were 
rejected. Eight percent of samples collected 
were rejected on this basis. Results from 
each specimen are averaged to give means 
for each core. The core means are averaged 
giving each unit weight to obtain the mean 
for each sampling site. The overall 
averages for each rock unit are calculated 
giving unit weight to the mean of each 
sampling site. 
ABITIBI DIKES 
In their unaltered state these dikes 
consist of 50-60 modal percent plagioclase, 
30% augite, 5-10% quartz and 5-7% 
opaques. The plagioclase is fresh and 
occurs as stubby to acicular laths up to 
2 mm long, bearing an ophitic to sub- 
ophitic relationship to the enclosing 
augite, which is mostly replaced by 
chlorite, brown and green amphibole, and 
biotite. Quartz occurs interstitially to the 
plagioclase and pyroxene. Magnetite was 
the original opaque mineral occurring as 
equant grains up to 1 mm in diameter 
with ilmenite exsolved around the margins 
and parallel to [111]. In most samples this 
primary magnetite has been totally al- 
tered, leaving only the ilmenite lamellae 
with a matrix of very fine-grained poorly 
reflecting material that could not be iden- 
tified in polished section. Small amounts 
(0.5%) of pyrite are present, commonly 
associated with biotite. Trace quantities 
of pyrrhotite and chalcopyrite are also 
observed. 
A study of the natural remanent 
magnetization (n.r.m.) of the Abitibi dikes 
has been described by Larochelle (1966). 
He reported a dominant westerly magneti- 
zation (W) with steep inclination from 
sampling sites immediately to the north- 
east of figure 1. In addition he reported 
two subordinate magnetizations, with 
directions to NNE and 8 W. The W 
magnetization has been assumed by most 
workers (e.g. Robertson and Fahrig 1971) 
to be the primary magnetization. McGlynn 
et al. (1975) and Pullaiah and Irving 
(1975) have recently questioned the age of 
magnetization of the Abitibi dikes, and 
Roy and Lapointe (1976) have argued 
that the similarity between directions of 
the NNE and SW magnetizations and 
what they regard as a secondary magneti- 
zation of the Nipissing diabase, suggests 
that they too are really secondary mag- 
160

FIG. 2.-Sampling of dikes and contacts in 
Munro Township. The magnetizations are 
distinguished by different symbols. At site M 
both Matachewan and Abitibi magnetizations 
are found. 
netizations. The NNE and SW magnetiza- 
tions could be a "Hudsonian" overprint 
acquired at about 1.8 Ga. The main 
problem however is to determine if the 
dominant W magnetization of the Abitibi 
dikes is truly the original magnetization 
acquired at the time the dikes were 
intruded. We now consider this question. 
Samples were taken from two dikes and 
from their baked margins at sites 6 and 7 
and (fig. 1) and in Munro Township (fig. 2). 
Both dikes have the typical W magnetiza- 
tion observed by Larochelle (1966). The 
thermal demagnetization curves, show 
wide variations, some diabase specimens 
(site 6) have discrete blocking temper- 
atures, others (site 3 and 2) have blocking 
temperatures distributed between room 
temperature and 500°C (fig. 3). During 
a.f. demagnetization the directions of

site 6 remain unchanged up to 400 Oe, but 
in higher fields they soon become random. 
During thermal demagnetization the direc- 
tions at site 6 remain constant up to 
550°C, are not greatly changed at 600°, 
but are random at 650°. The corresponding 
decay curve is square-shouldered, with 
blocking temperatures predominantly be- 
tween 550 and 650°C. This indicates that 
magnetite is the main carrier, but that 
hematite is present also in small quantities. 
This is confirmed by studies of polished 
sections from site 6. Large grains of 
magnetite are seen to contain very fine 
exsolved lamellae of ilmenite, rims of 
ilmenite, and also fine exsolution lamellae

of hematite. The directions in the baked 
granite adjoining the diabase dike at 
site 6 are parallel to those in the diabase 
(compare means at sites 6 and 7 in 
table 1), and the remanent coercivities 
exceed 1,000 Oe (fig. 4). The blocking 
temperatures are distributed between 300 
to 600°C with a small component retained 
at 600°C. This indicates that fine-grained 
hematite is the carrier of the remanence. 
In polished section the oxides are seen to 
consist of 0.5 to 1 mm diameter magnetite 
grains, now partially altered, and with 
ilmenite lamellae oriented parallel to 
(111). Chromite also occurs in association 
with altered sphene. 
The dike in Munro Township has been 
studied in more detail at a point where it 
cuts a N-S trending Matachewan dike 
which is itself cutting one of the gabbroic 
bodies referred to above as having been 
emplaced along an ESE-striking fault 
(fig. 2). Samples have been taken from the 
dike itself (sites 1, 2, and 3) from its 
contact with Matachewan diabase and 
outwards along the Matachewan dike for a 
distance of 150 m. The remanent coercive 
forces in this Abitibi dike are rather low, 
the median destructive field (m.d.f.) being 
less than 100 Oe (fig. 3, sites 2 and 3). The 
blocking temperatures are generally dis- 
tributed between room temperature and 
600°C, with a concentration between 
550°C and 600°C in specimens at the 
chilled contact (fig. 3, site 3). This indicates 
that magnetite or titano-magnetite are 
carriers of the remanence. In polished 
section, much of the magnetite has been 
altered to a fine-grained poorly reflecting 
material containing lamellae of original 
exsolution ilmenite, but localized areas of 
the original magnetite remain unaffected. 
In addition ultrafine (1 micron) blebs of an 
oxide that may be magnetite, but which 
are too fine to identify with certainty, 
occur along the cleavage planes of altered 
pyroxene. Warmed Matachewan diabase 
within 30 m of the contact has the same 
W direction, and square-shouldered ther- 
mal decay curves with blocking temper- 
atures between 550 and 600°C (fig. 4, 
sites 4 and 5). High remanent coercive 
forces are present and the directions are 
little changed in fields up to 1,000 Oe. At 
site M (fig. 2) 80 m from the contact two 
specimen cores were collected within 5 m 
of one another. One gave a direction 
290, +63 and the other a direction 
209, +03 corresponding to the Abitibi W 
and Matachewan (see below) directions 
respectively. Traced southward along the 
Matachewan dike the W magnetization is 
retained for a distance of 80 m, beyond 
which typical Matachewan magnetizations 
occur. Clearly during the intrusion of 
Abitibi diabase, remagnetization on a 
regional scale did not occur, but was 
confined locally to a zone about 80 m wide 
162

### page_7
EVIDENCE OF THE ARCHEAN GEOMAGNETIC FIELD 
adjacent to the diabase itself. It follows 
also that the W magnetization was 
acquired during cooling, and is the 
primary magnetization as previous workers 
have assumed it to be. Using the above 
thermal demagnetization results and the 
approximations of Pullaiah et al. (1975), 
the temperature attained at a distance of 
about 80 m may be estimated to be about 
400°C. Consideration of Jaeger's (1957) 
cooling curves applied to a diabase dyke 
equal in thickness to the dike studied by 
us (100 m) and intruding material of 
similar conductivity and density to itself, 
suggests that the maximum temperature 
reached at a point 80 m from the contact 
would be 360°C higher than the temper- 
ature of the country rocks at the time of 
intrusion. Provided that the temperature 
of the country rocks was low, this is 
consistent with the conclusions from the 
magnetization studies. The change from 
Abitibi to Matachewan directions ap- 
parently occurs suddenly within a matter 
of metres since at site M of figure 2 both 
magnetizations occur. There is no evidence 
of a transition zone where both magnetiza- 
tions occur, and in neither sample is there 
a change during demagnetization from W 
Abitibi to Matachewan directions; the 
magnetization appears to be either com- 
pletely Abitibi W or completely Mata- 
chewan. This is consistent with the 
observed presence of very narrow discrete 
range of blocking temperatures. Unfor- 
tunately, because of heavy bush, sampling 
on either side of site M was not practicable. 
Mean directions in all cores from 
Abitibi diabase and contact rocks are 
shown in figure 5, and summarized in 
table 1. The directions in contacts and 
diabase are in excellent agreement. 
MATACHEWAN DIKES 
The Matachewan diabase dikes form an 
extensive swarm of north-trending vertical 
dikes (fig. 1). The samples studied by us 
resemble the Abitibi dikes in that they are 
composed of 50-60% plagioclase, 30% 
augite, 5-10% quartz and granophyric 
FIG. 5.-Directions observed in core samples 
(mean of two specimens from each core) from 
Abitibi dikes and warmed contacts rocks. The 
primitive is the present horizontal. P is the 
direction of the present field. All directions are 
downwards. 
intergrowths, and 5o% opaques. The 
plagioclase is lath-like, but the augite 
differs from that in the Abitibi dikes in 
that in addition to developing interstitially 
to the plagioclase, much of it occurs also 
as equant grains. The principal oxide 
mineral is magnetite, now largely altered 
to a fine grained poorly reflecting material, 
and containing ilmenite lamellae and rims. 
The remanent magnetization of the 
Matachewan dikes has been studied pre- 
viously by Strangway (1964) and Fahrig 
et al. (1965) who carried out magnetic 
cleaning in fields of about 100 Oe, but who 
reported no thermal or contact studies. 
These workers found directions of opposite 
polarities, but they were not antiparallel, 
the misalignment being on average 40°, 
and in the sense expected from incomplete 
removal of viscous magnetizations caused 
by the present geomagnetic field. Incom- 
plete cleaning in these early studies is 
probably the cause of the misalignment, 
because we find that after cleaning in 
fields of 300 or 400 Oe there is no evidence 
of misalignment.

We have sampled Matachewan diabase 
at 11 sites (figs. 1, 2, and 9). Ten sites have 
southerly directions and one site (site 11) 
has northerly directions. Typical results 
from demagnetization of rocks with 
164 
southerly magnetizations are shown in 
figure 6. At site 8 in Munro township 
(fig. 2), the diabase samples have square- 
shouldered demagnetization curves with 
blocking temperatures between 500 and

FIG. 6.-Demagnetization of Matachewan 
diabase (site 8), baked Archean gabbro adjacent 
to diabase (site 9), and Archean gabbro 65 m 
from diabase (site 10). See Fig. 2. Thermal decay 
and corresponding directions are given above, 
and a.f. decay and corresponding directions

600°C. The a.f. demagnetization curves 
fall smoothly. During both a.f. and 
thermal demagnetizations there were small 
shifts in inclination, owing to the removal 
of magnetizations along the present geo- 
magnetic field. The blocking temperature 
indicates that the magnetization is carried 
by fine-grained titanium-free magnetite. 
In polished section the oxides are seen to 
consist of fine-grained poorly reflective 
material pseudomorphing magnetite with 
ilmenite exsolution lamellae, very fine 
lamellae of magnetite localized along the 
cleavage planes of altered pyroxene, and a 
fine powder, probably magnetite, that is 
visible in transmitted light but not 
apparently in polished section. 
The directions in the baked gabbro 
(site 9 in Archean gabbro) have an 
excellent end-point between 200 and 
600 Oe, and the directions do not change 
greatly in a.f. up to 1,000 Oe (fig. 6). The 
baked gabbro has square-shouldered ther- 
mal demagnetization curves with some 
blocking temperatures exceeding 600°C. 
The thermal demagnetization curves of 
unbaked Archean gabbro (site 10, fig. 2) at 
a distance of 60 m from the Matachewan 
diabase, fall almost linearly with temper- 
ature. Opaque oxides include large skeletal 
grains of altered magnetite, containing 
patches and lamellae of ilmenite, and rare 
inclusions of hematite and chalcopyrite. A 
fine oxide, that could not be identified, is 
also associated with altered pyroxene. The 
directions however remain approximately 
constant and are similar to those observed 
in the Matachewan diabase and their 
immediate contacts (fig. 6, upper part). 
Elsewhere there is a strong contrast 
between the directions of magnetization 
in Archean basement, and the Matachewan 
diabase and their warmed contacts. At 
site 11 the diabase intrudes the Kamiskotia 
gabbro (fig. 7 and 9, below). The gabbro 
samples were collected at distances 1 to 
12 m west of the dyke contact. The 
directions in both the diabase and baked 
gabbro are slightly east of north, and are 
reversed (within the errors) from the 
southerly directions of figure 6 (table 1). 
The blocking temperatures are confined to 
a discrete interval between 550 and 600°C. 
During a.f. and thermal demagnetization 
the directions show excellent end-points. 
The directions in baked gabbro are close 
to those from the diabase (compare sites 
11 and 12 in table 1). The directions in the 
Kamiskotia complex (see next section) are 
about 90° away. This again shows that 
remagnetization caused by intrusion of 
Matachewan diabase is local, and that the 
magnetization of the Matachewan diabase 
and their immediate contact rocks was 
acquired at the time of cooling at -2.6 Ga. 
The contrasting behaviour of similar 
directions in diabase and host rocks at 
Munro, and the very different directions

In the area sampled by us the complex 
is gabbroic, composed of about 50 modal 
percent plagioclase, 40% augite, 5% of an 
alteration thought to be after hypersthene,

slightly elongated (5 mm x 1.5 m), but

FIG. 9.-Sketch map of Kamiskotia complex

and (001) of what is thought to be altered 
hypersthene. The oxides consist of a fine 
grained alteration after magnetite, with 
ilmenite at grain boundaries. Irregular 
blebs of pyrite occur along the cleavage 
planes of augite, together with very fine 
flakes of an oxide, thought to be hematite. 
The intrusion is heavily timbered and 
not readily accessible, and water for 
drilling is absent over much of the outcrop. 
Sampling was confined to the northwestern 
part of the intrusion where samples from 
seven sites were obtained (fig. 9). Typical 
decay curves are shown in figure 10. The 
initial directions were usually near the 
present field, but during demagnetization 
they migrate to the west-northwest, and 
this direction is retained after demagneti- 
zation in fields up to 1,000 Oe. The 
thermal decay curves have a two-stepped 
form. Magnetizations with blocking tem- 
peratures distributed between 200 and 
450°C have directions along the present 
field, and are presumably viscous com- 
ponents imposed by the present field. 
There is also a magnetization with 
blocking temperatures between 520 and 
600°C and it is this that has the west- 
northwest directions. The carrier of the 
latter magnetization is evidently magne- 
tite. After magnetic cleaning the directions 
in all samples are well-grouped (fig. 11), 
and this magnetization predates the

intrusion of the Matachewan dikes because 
it is only immediately adjacent to the

that in the dikes. 
DUNDONALD SILL 
The Dundonald sill is a simple differen- 
tiated sill ranging from peridotite at the 
base through pyroxenite to a gabbro 
which contains occasional zones of grano- 
phyric gabbro (Naldrett and Mason 1968). 
Since layering within the sill correlates 
closely with interflow contacts in the 
enclosing volcanics, it is thought to have 
crystallized with a sub-horizontal orienta- 
tion, but it has since been deformed into a 
W-shape consisting of two synclines 
flanking a central anticline (fig. 12). The 
peridotites are mostly completely ser- 
pentinized, but pseudomorphic textures

### page_12
E. IRVING AND A. J. NALDRETT 
FIG. 11.-Directions of magnetization in 
samples (mean of 2 specimens from each core 
sample) from Kamiskotia complex and Dun- 
donald sill. P is direction of the present field. 
The primitive is the present horizontal plane. 
indicate that it was originally composed of 
olivine and augite in the proportions of 
4 to 1. The pyroxenites consist of 60-95 
modal percent of relatively fresh diopsidic 
augite with chloritic alteration after 
plagioclase. Fresh to moderately altered 
intercumulus plagioclase is common in the 
upper part of the pyroxenite horizon 
towards the contact with the gabbro, 
although it is usually saussuritized. The 
gabbros consist of cumulus plagioclase 
(now partially saussuritized), cumulus 
augite, and up to 10% of altered cumulus 
magnetite containing both large and 
extremely fine exsolution lamellae of 
ilmenite. The proportion of magnetite 
decreases upwards to less than 5% in the 
upper half of the gabbro. 
Samples were obtained from eight sites 
from the north limb and three sites from 
the south limb (fig. 12). Opaque minerals 
in the peridotite are primary chromite and 
secondary magnetite, distributed through- 
out the serpentine as a fine dusting, and 
also as small granules concentrated along 
cross-cutting serpentine veinlets. Chromite 
is the principal oxide at the base of the 
pyroxenite horizon, but this.gives way to 
magnetite in the central and upper 
portions of the unit. While the chromite is 
fresh in all samples examined, the magne- 
tite is largely altered and contains fine 
lamellae of ilmenite. Fine flakes (<3 
microns) of oxide, probably magnetite, 
occur along the cleavage in the pyroxenes. 
The main oxide in the gabbro is magnetite, 
occurring as 1 mm diameter grains 
containing up to 40% exsolved ilmenite, 
some of it exsolved on such a fine scale as 
to subdivide the host magnetite into areas 
a few tens of microns in dimensions. The 
magnetite is now largely altered. 
Coherent magnetization was obtained 
from four of the five pyroxenite sites 
sampled and one oxide-rich gabbro site 
distinguished by solid dots in figure 12. 
During a.f. demagnetization the directions 
migrate away from the present field to a 
west-northwest direction and remain ap- 
proximately constant up to 1,000 Oe 
(fig. 13). The thermal decay curves show a 
narrow range of blocking temperatures 
between 500 and 600°C, suggesting that 
fine-grained titanium-free magnetite is the 
carrier of the remanence. There is only one 
sample with coherent magnetization from 
the south limb, so that a fold test cannot 
be made. The directions in all samples 
after cleaning are shown in figure 11. The 
directions differ strongly from directions 
in Matachewan diabase, but are similar 
(although more scattered) to those of the 
Kamiskotia complex, indicating that the 
remanence is pre-Matachewan in age. 
ULTRAMAFIC LAVA 
Ultramafic lavas were sampled from the 
locality in Munro Township described by 
Pyke et al. (1973). Many of the flows 
consist of a basal zone (B zone) rich in 
cumulus olivine, overlain by a zone (A 
zone) composed of skeletal olivine and 
pyroxene displaying spinifex texture. 
Other flows do not show this zonation and 
are characterized by a uniform distribution 
of olivine phenocrysts. Although fresh 
olivine and pyroxene occur, secondary

Sampling covered a stratigraphic interval

flows. 
Magnetizations with both discrete and 
distributed blocking temperatures (re- 
ferred to as groups I and II respectively) 
occur. Group I samples have blocking 
temperatures between 450 and 550°C, 
and, in specimen 26, between 550 and 
650°C (fig. 14). The remanent coercive 
force of group I samples is rather high, the 
median destructive fields ranging from 200 
to 400 Oe. Directional changes during 
magnetic cleaning are shown in figure 15 
(right-hand side). In specimen 26 the 
directions with respect to present horizon- 
tal are initially nearly vertical and 
directed upward, and remain there during 
demagnetization up to 500 Oe. In specimen 
15 the directions move into this direction 
after demagnetization in fields of about 
200 Oe. These properties suggest that the 
carrier of the remanent magnetization in 
the group I specimens is low-titanium 
magnetite, or hematite in specimen 26. As 
mentioned above, polished section study 
revealed the presence of both magnetite 
and hematite in most samples. We were 
unable to distinguish any anomalous 
amounts of hematite in sample 26 to

DISCUSSION 
The results show that the magnetiza- 
tions of the Abitibi and Matachewan 
dikes were acquired during cooling and 
have not been altered subsequently. The 
magnetization of the Kamiskotia complex 
was acquired prior to the intrusion of 
the Matachewan dikes and is therefore 
Archean. The magnetization of Dundonald 
sill is less easily interpreted, but the 
directions are similar to those in the 
Kamiskotia complex and therefore it is 
probably that its magnetization is also

### page_15
171 EVIDENCE OF THE ARCHEAN GEOMAGNETIC FIELD 
ULTRABASIC LAVA SITE 23 
FIG. 15.-Directions of magnetization in Group I samples of ultrabasic lava, site 23. Cleaned 
directions in all specimens are given on the left, and typical changes in direction during a.f. de- 
magnetization in samples 15 and 26. P is the present filed direction. The primitive is the horizontal. 
Archean. The Dundonald sill magnetiza- 
tion is probably post-deformational, but 
this deformation may have occurred soon 
after formation so the magnetization may 
also date from that time. Rocks with high 
blocking temperatures in a range 500 to 
600°C and square-shouldered demagnetiza- 
tion curves occur in the Dundonald and 
Kamiskotia bodies indicating that this 
material is unlikely to have been reset by 
heating during regional metamorphism to 
the prehnite-pumpellyite grade prevalent 
in this region (Pullaiah et al. 1975). The 
group I samples from the ultrabasic lavas 
give consistent directions with high block- 
ing temperatures, but until results are 
available from other localities no weight 
can be placed on them and they are not 
considered further. 
A summary of the results is given in 
table 2. The Archean poles together with 
those from Aphebian rocks are plotted in 
figure 16. A smooth curve can be drawn 
through them, the one exception being the 
pole for the Dogrib dikes which falls near 
Japan. A prominent bend in the curve 
occurs in NE Siberia at about -2.3 Ga. 
To conform with the classification of 
Irving and McGlynn (1975) we may refer 
to this bend as hairpin 50. The polar path 
following this bend is referred to as 
track 5 and the path before as track 6. 
Track 5 has been discussed previously 
(Irving and Lapointe 1975; McGlynn 
et al. 1975; Roy et al. 1975; Irving and 
McGlynn 1976; Roy and Lapointe 1976). 
Track 6 is the first recorded attempt to 
provide an APW curve for the late 
Archean based on magnetizations that are 
of Archean age. It is obviously very 
tentative indeed, both in form and 
timing. The age calibration at -2.6 Ga is 
given by the age of the Matachewan 
dikes. The calibration at approximately 
-2.8 Ga for the Dundonald sill and 
Kamiskotia complex is suggested, very 
tentatively, on the basis of the agreement 
of their poles with that for the Stillwater

(1966) is given. In entries 2 and 3 the results from the two Abitibi dikes described herein are combined with those of entry 1. 
There are four previous results from Matachewan dikes normal and reversed directions given by Fahrig et al. (1965) and 
Strangway (1964). In entry 4 these four results are averaged irrespective of sign giving each unit weight N = 4. In this 
earlier work no breakdown by sites has been given so no combination with the new data given herein can be given. In 
entries 5 and 6 the present results are summarized from Matachewan dikes. In entries 11 and 12 the directions are corrected 
for bedding tilt. In entries 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 unit weight is given to sites. 
complex. Obviously this is not a satis- 
factory calibration of track 6 but seems 
the most reasonable on the basis of the 
present scanty evidence. 
One of the main problems in Pre- 
cambrian work is to determine whether 
the remanence directions should be referred 
(a) to the horizontal at the time the rock 
was formed on the assumption that the 
magnetization was acquired prior to 
deformation, or (b) to present horizontal 
on the assumption that it was acquired 
after deformation, or (c) to some other 
plane on the assumption that the magneti- 
zation was acquired at some intermediate 
stage of deformation. (This problem does 
not of course arise in studies of vertically 
inclined diabase dikes.) If (a) or (c) are the 
proper procedures, then study of deformed 
rocks of this very great age (and most are 
deformed) is severely limited, because in 
most situations the correct reference 
plane cannot be accurately determined. 
One of the redeeming features of Pre- 
cambrian work in the Canadian Shield, 
which apparently makes this aspect of 
paleomagnetic work simpler than it might 
at first sight appear, is that coherent 
polar tracks can be obtained when 
directions are referred to present hori- 
zontal. This amounts to a negative fold 
test on a continent-wide scale. It is a 
feature, not only of highly deformed and 
metamorphosed terrains where it is to be 
expected (Ueno and Irving 1976; Mc- 
Williams and Dunlop 1976), but also of 
rocks that have undergone little or no 
alteration (McGlynn et al. 1974). In the 
present context an item of interest is the 
agreement between pole for the Stillwater 
complex (SU) and those for the Kamiskotia 
and Dundonald bodies, when all the 
directions are referred to present horizontal 
(fig. 16). It is therefore possible that 
the present horizontal (hypothesis (b)) is 
the correct plane of reference, and that the 
bodies have not undergone very much 
relative movement since they were magne- 
tized. This point if substantiated by 
further observations, is of considerable 
interest, because it implies little or no 
relative movement between the Stillwater 
block and the Superior Province. 
There is no polar bend (or hairpin) 
associated with the Kenoran Orogeny. 
This is different from Proterozoic and 
Phanerozoic orogenies that are character- 
ized by polar loops and hairpins. This 
result could mean that the Kenoran 
Orogeny is entirely unlike Phanerozoic and

Proterozoic orogenies, or it could simply 
reflect the inadequacy of the record 
available at present. There does, however, 
appear to be a hairpin at about -2.3 Ga 
and this could be the polar signature of a 
mid-Aphebian orogeny. Further evidence 
for this is to be found in the divergence of 
the Dogrib pole (-2.6 Ga) from track 6. 
If this is indicative of movement between 
the Slave and Superior Provinces then 
this movement appears to have been 
mid-Aphebian in age and was completed 
by about -2.1 Ga, because poles of this 
age from Slave and Superior available at 
the present time and are in substantial 
agreement (McGlynn et al. 1975).
